answer.why: As an insider, "Confirmed & Substantive" made me laugh straight away. It is the exact wording you wait for after probation or a promotion, and nobody outside the service would think to use it as a title. It tells me the developer actually knows the world. "Minister Salary" is the obvious hook, but it reads like a clickbait headline for a national grievance, and I get enough of that in the news cycle. I would still tap the first one out of curiosity, but it would make me brace for wrong details.
answer.expect_minister_salary: A satirical, slightly cynical game about the million-dollar ministerial pay debate. I would expect a punchy gimmick, with you chasing the top job and the pay package, and a fair amount of getting the benchmarks wrong. It would be easy to sell to a general audience but probably shallow on how the service really works, with politics as the goal and not much of the grind in between.
answer.expect_confirmed_substantive: A dry, insider-flavoured game about the actual career grind: probation, appraisals, grades, postings, waiting to be confirmed in a post. I would expect gentle humour in the details, like the meeting about the meeting, and a game that respects the process more than the payoff. It would be a niche title, and outsiders would probably find the name baffling, but it would feel made by someone who has sat through the cycles.

worst_moment.what: Seeing every last resident at Tuesday MPS and then watching STAND fall anyway. The repeated PQ and walkabout years blurred together and the feedback contradicted my choices.

callbacks_noticed.earlier_choice: Y2: nominated the quiet officer who does real work
callbacks_noticed.came_back_as: She became Deputy Secretary, which I noted as goodwill paying off

callbacks_noticed.came_back_as: The RO became Perm Sec, which fit how patronage and trust travel in the service

answer.held_back_by: Mostly nothing. I reached PM at 59 with Integrity 100, so the run rewarded candour and quiet fixing almost too neatly. The only drag was STAND sliding for reasons the game never explained.
answer.ending_fair_why: Candour and trust-building paid off throughout, and the formula was stated on the card. The ending matched my choices, though the STAND decline never resolved and the Y3 pilot and the Tuesday man never visibly came back, which left loose ends.
answer.chase_next: A run where I take the tempting choices, shade the truth or chase ranking, to see whether a lower-integrity path ends at a different office or a different pay figure. I also want to see the Y3 pilot and the Tuesday man payoff.
answer.play_again_why: The late years repeated themselves and the clear rule was candour pays. I would come back after a break to try a worse-behaved career, not right now.

tone_breaks.line: The formula pays you twice the entry-grade minister's salary
tone_breaks.note: Earlier I noted the game's figures seem inconsistent. Real ministerial pay is benchmarked to a basket of top earners with a discount, not a simple multiple like this, so this reads as simplified or wrong.

tone_breaks.line: RETIRED AS Prime Minister AT AGE 59
tone_breaks.note: Retiring at 59 right after becoming PM, with no years actually playing as PM, felt abrupt. The top job got one card and no year to play.

answer.title_fit_why: The run ended on the pay formula and lifetime earnings, and the ending card is framed around salary. The grades and tea were more textured than the title suggests, but the money is what the game hangs on.
